The notebooks below accompany Unit 5. They are ordinary Jupyter
notebooks and need only `numpy` (plus `matplotlib` for the plots, and
`control`/`slycot` for a few of the continuous-time models); open them
in JupyterLab, VS Code, or any notebook environment. A lighter,
dependency-free Python version of the core recursion is in
[`riccati.py`](riccati.py) -- see [`README.md`](README.md).

## Finite-horizon LQR for a double integrator

The worked example of the lecture: the finite-horizon cost
$\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}x_k^\intercal Qx_k+u_k^\intercal Ru_k+x_h^\intercal Q_hx_h$
applied to a double integrator. Every parameter is exposed, so it is the
one to open first if you want to feel what $Q$, $R$, $Q_h$ and the
horizon $h$ actually do to the closed loop -- raise $R$ and watch the
input get lazier, raise $Q_h$ and watch the terminal state get pulled in
harder.

[Download `A_5_LQfinhorizondoubleintegrator.ipynb`](A_5_LQfinhorizondoubleintegrator.ipynb){download="A_5_LQfinhorizondoubleintegrator.ipynb"}

## Riccati equations and the infinite-horizon limit

The same double integrator, but with the horizon pushed out: the
notebook iterates the backward Riccati recursion and shows
$P_k\to\bar P$ and $K_k\to\bar K$, so the solution of the *algebraic*
Riccati equation appears as the limit of the finite-horizon one. This is
the computational counterpart of the convergence argument in the notes.

[Download `A_5_Riccatiequations.ipynb`](A_5_Riccatiequations.ipynb){download="A_5_Riccatiequations.ipynb"}

## Reference tracking with LQR

Stabilization drives the state to zero; tracking asks it to follow a
reference $r_k$. Minimizing
$\sum_k\|Mx_k-r_k\|^2+u_k^\intercal Ru_k$ by dynamic programming gives an
optimal policy of the affine form $u_k=K_kx_k+L_k$, where -- and this is
the point worth taking away -- the gains $K_k$ are *exactly* those of the
stabilization problem, and all the reference information is carried by
the feedforward term $L_k$.

[Download `A_5_N_referencetrackinglqr.ipynb`](A_5_N_referencetrackinglqr.ipynb){download="A_5_N_referencetrackinglqr.ipynb"}

## LQR for the inverted pendulum

The infinite-horizon regulator applied to the linearized
inverted-pendulum-on-a-cart, under full state feedback -- the same plant
that returns in Unit 6 once the state has to be estimated rather than
measured. A good reference point for how much the LQG controller of the
next unit gives up when only a noisy cart position is available.

[Download `A_5_K_LQRinvertedpendulum.ipynb`](A_5_K_LQRinvertedpendulum.ipynb){download="A_5_K_LQRinvertedpendulum.ipynb"}

## Positioning a flexible head-disk drive

A genuinely industrial example: positioning the read/write head of a disk
drive, where the arm is flexible, so the torque applied at the base and
the angle of the head are separated by a lightly damped resonance. The
model is the two-inertia system of Franklin, Powell and Emami-Naeini,
and it shows what LQR does with a plant whose dynamics actively fight a
fast response.

[Download `A_5_K_PositioningHeadDisk.ipynb`](A_5_K_PositioningHeadDisk.ipynb){download="A_5_K_PositioningHeadDisk.ipynb"}

## Tracking an ellipsoidal trajectory under disturbances

A particle with first-order velocity dynamics in the plane is asked to
follow an ellipsoidal reference while random disturbances push it off
course, and the cost penalizes the variance of the tracking error. It
combines the reference-tracking formulation above with the stochastic
setting that opens Unit 6.

[Download `A_5_K_Tracking_lqr.ipynb`](A_5_K_Tracking_lqr.ipynb){download="A_5_K_Tracking_lqr.ipynb"}

## Smooth trajectory generation with LQR

The least obvious use of the machinery in this unit. Given $N$ waypoints
in 3D and the times at which they must be met, the task is to produce a
trajectory through them that is smooth up to a given derivative order.
Posing this as an LQR problem -- the control being the highest
derivative, the cost penalizing deviation from a piecewise-linear
interpolant -- turns a trajectory-design question into exactly the
Riccati recursion of this unit. Worth reading as evidence that "linear
quadratic" is a much wider hammer than "drive the state to zero".

[Download `A_5_A_LQR_Smoothing.ipynb`](A_5_A_LQR_Smoothing.ipynb){download="A_5_A_LQR_Smoothing.ipynb"}
